data.claim: A multi-line quoted string stops _split from treating ; as a command separator, so commands after the ; are never matched.
data.falsifier: check('echo a; git push origin main; python3 -c "<newline>print(1)"') returns a Refusal naming git push instead of None.
data.mechanism: _split tokenizes each physical line separately. A quote spanning a newline makes shlex raise ValueError on the line that opens it, so the line.split() fallback is used, which leaves ; glued to the preceding word (-q;, main;), and the after-; commands are swallowed into the first command.
data.probe: python3 - run _split/check on the repro line in the worktree
data.probe_output: split -> [['echo','a;','git','push','origin','main;','python3','-c','"']]; check -> None (one-line form is refused)
data.question: Does the forbidden-command guard miss commands after a semicolon when the line holds a multi-line quoted string?

evidence.note: CONFIRMED research Ree9a478729: a multi-line quoted string stops _split from treating ; as a separator (probe: _split('echo a; git push origin main; python3 -c "<nl>print(1)"') -> [['echo','a;','git','push','origin','main;','python3','-c','"']], check -> None while the one-line form is refused). Fixed by splitting logical lines at quotes-aware newlines first.

chunk_findings.detail: A newline inside double quotes is treated as data for the whole remainder of the quote, but the shell still runs command substitutions and backticks there. Input `echo "$(\ngit push origin main\n)"` (or the same with backticks) used to be split on the physical newline, so `git push origin main` was a separate line and refused. `_logical_lines` now keeps that newline inside the `"` span and hands shlex one quoted word, so `_check` does not see `git`. The new tests only cover `python3 -c "..."` data and never this case, so they miss the regression.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_logical_lines

chunk_findings.detail: Inside double quotes, POSIX/bash delete a backslash-newline before the text is parsed, so `echo "$\` + newline + `(git push origin main)"` and `echo "\`` + newline + `git push origin main`"` both run `git push` as a command substitution. `mark_dquote` (and the same `\\` branch in `mark_command`) consumes that pair as literal data and never re-reads `$`/`(` or the backtick, so the newline is not a cut and `_check` never sees `git`. The old physical-newline split refused the second line; `test_refused_command_substitution_multiline` only covers a `$` already adjacent to `(`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_strip_continuations` treats every `'` as a single-quoted span and, if the closer is missing, stops stripping backslash-newlines for the rest of the text. A `'` inside double quotes is literal in bash, so `echo "it's $\` + newline + `(git push origin main)"` (and `echo "'$\` + newline + `(git push origin main)"`) still joins to `$(git push origin main)` and runs it. After the stripper leaves the `\`-newline in place, `dquote` sees `$` then `\` and skips the newline instead of a `(`, so `_substitutions` never records `git push` and `_check` returns None. The regression strings have no `'` before the continuation, so they do not catch this.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:119

chunk_findings.detail: `command` sets `cut` on every newline in a `$(...)` or backtick body, and `_logical_lines` uses that same array to split the outer script. Those newlines separate only the inner command. For `echo "$(echo x\n)"; git push origin main`, bash runs `git push`, but the cut breaks the outer line into `echo "$(echo x` and `)"; git push origin main`. `shlex` (posix, the second line) treats the leading `"` as an unclosed quote and swallows `; git push origin main` as data, and the substitution body is only `echo x\n`, so `_check` returns None. The same split happens for any forbidden command after `;` following a double-quoted substitution that contains a newline.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:146

chunk_findings.detail: `_strip_continuations` treats every `'` as a quote delimiter and never a backslash-escaped literal, so a `\<newline>` that bash still removes (line continuation is decided only for an unquoted backslash) is left in the text. `_scan` then skips that pair as an ordinary escape and never sees `$` adjacent to `(`. Given `echo \'$` + `\` + newline + `(git push origin main)`, bash joins to `echo \'$` + `$(git push origin main)` and runs `git push`; both `_substitutions` and `_commands` miss it, so `_check` returns None.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:119

chunk_findings.detail: Substitution bodies are taken only from the original string and then from those bodies. A `-c` argument is `_split` but never passed to `_substitutions`, so a forbidden command that is not argv[0] of the `-c` script is invisible. `sh -c 'echo $(git push origin main)'` and `sh -c 'echo "$(git push origin main)"'` run `git push` and `_check` returns None, while the same `echo "$(git push origin main)"` at top level is refused.

chunk_findings.detail: `_strip_continuations` still treats every `'` as a quote start and never a backslash-escaped literal, and a fake single-quoted span keeps `\<newline>`. Bash removes an unquoted backslash-newline before quotes apply. Given `echo \'$` + `\` + newline + `(git push origin main)`, bash joins to `echo '$(git push origin main)` and runs `git push`. After this function the continuation remains, `_scan` then skips `\` and the newline as an ordinary escape so `$` is never adjacent to `(`, and both `_substitutions` and `_commands` miss it. The added scanner does not fix that path; the strip still runs first.

chunk_findings.detail: `-c` scripts are still only `_split`, never passed to `_substitutions`. Outer single quotes hide `$(...)` from the top-level scan (correct for the outer shell), and shlex then hands the inner shell the script `echo $(git push origin main)`. `sh -c 'echo $(git push origin main)'` and `sh -c 'echo "$(git push origin main)"'` both run `git push`, while the same `echo "$(git push origin main)"` at top level is refused. Nesting `_substitutions` only over bodies already taken from the original string does not close this.

chunk_findings.detail: `find_body` lost the old `elif c == "\\":` skip, so a backslash-escaped closer is treated as the end of the command substitution. For example, in `echo $(echo \)\n); git push origin main` (the `)` after `\` is escaped, and the following newline is inside the real `$()` body), `if c == closer: return k` returns the escaped `)`, not the real closing `)`. The next newline is then seen as a top-level newline and cut there, even though it must remain inside the substitution body. This is exactly the “newline inside `$()` is split out of the outer line” failure this change is meant to prevent, and it can make the matcher inspect the wrong fragment instead of the actual command. Old `command` skipped `\` plus its next character; this regression removes that behavior.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:find_body

chunk_findings.detail: `find_body` treats the first `)` / backtick as the closer and never skips a backslash escape (the old `command()` walker did; the new outer loop still does). Inside double quotes that is a bypass: bash still runs the substitution because `\)` is not the closer, but `dquote_end` resumes in the double-quoted span and swallows the rest as data. Given `echo "$(echo \); git push origin main)"`, bash executes `git push origin main`, the body stored is only `echo \`, and no later scan sees `git push`, so the guard allows it. The same early close happens for `` echo "`echo \`; git push origin main`" ``.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:158
